faqs.q: There is a raccoon denning above my St. Matthews ceiling. Will you release it somewhere wild?
faqs.a: We cannot promise a release, because the state does not allow routine relocation — a captured raccoon must be destroyed or moved only under a separate department permit. What works in St. Matthews is getting the animal out and keeping the next one out: one-way eviction doors, removal under depredation rules where needed, and steel sealing at the roofline. Because raccoons lead SC Department of Public Health rabies results, we also treat attic contamination seriously and clean latrine spots rather than leaving them sealed in.

faqs.q: We keep finding snakes around our St. Matthews house. What can be done?
faqs.a: Most snakes we are called about in St. Matthews are harmless rat snakes, black racers, and garter snakes following rodents and frogs around farm-town center. The ones that change the call are the copperhead, which is statewide and the venomous snake we encounter most in the Upstate and Midlands. Identify first, from a safe distance: keep kids and pets inside, do not try to move or kill it, note where it went, and call us. Venomous snakes are safety-and-identification work, not a guaranteed capture, and the lasting fix is usually habitat — clearing brush, woodpiles, and rodent shelter near the house.

faqs.q: What does a wildlife removal job in St. Matthews actually involve?
faqs.a: It starts with the inspection, and the scope grows or shrinks with what that inspection finds around farm-town center: how many entry points the animal has opened, whether young are present, and how much exclusion the roofline and crawlspace need. A single squirrel entry sealed in a day is a small job; a raccoon family with latrine cleanup and a full roofline seal is a larger one. We walk you through each item we find before the work is set, so the scope you approve is the scope we do.

St. Matthews.wildlife_intro:
In St. Matthews, most of our work starts around the farm-town center and the Sandhills fields around the county seat. More than anything else, we are called for raccoons in brick-ranch attics and gray squirrels chewing into soffits.

Brick ranches from the 1960s and 1970s, older in-town homes near the center, and fast-growing subdivisions at the edges give this housing stock three distinct generations of rooflines to inspect. River and lake country surrounds these neighborhoods — creeks, coves, and wooded drains run behind the subdivisions — giving raccoons, squirrels, and bats a covered route to almost every roofline.

The last step on a St. Matthews call is a walk-around with the homeowner: each entry we sealed, each burrow we screened, and what to watch for when the seasons turn.

faqs.q: There is a dead animal smell in my Cameron walls. What should I do?
faqs.a: Call us rather than opening walls at random. Our crew locates the carcass — a dead raccoon, opossum, or squirrel in a wall void or crawlspace is the usual source — removes it, and sanitizes the area. Carcasses of raccoons, skunks, and bats are handled with rabies precautions in line with Department of Public Health guidance, and we check how the animal got in so the entry is sealed as part of the same visit.

faqs.q: Are armadillos really established around Cameron?
faqs.a: Yes. Nine-banded armadillos are established throughout the entirety of South Carolina, and around here they burrow under porches, driveways, and crawlspace edges and root up lawns hunting grubs and worms. We trap the animals working your property and backfill and screen the burrow openings, because an open burrow in this soil is quickly claimed by the next armadillo — or by a skunk or opossum.

Cameron.wildlife_intro:
Our crew works Cameron from the rail corridor and farm roads toward the Congaree bottoms. The homes here sit in Sandhills farms and pine land east of the Congaree River floodplain, with swamp hardwoods along the river and lake, and that habitat explains most of what we find: raccoons, opossums, armadillos, gray squirrels account for the bulk of our Cameron calls, moving between the wild ground and the housing along the same creeks, field edges, and canopy streets every night.

Older farm-town homes and rural farmhouses, largely on pier foundations and crawlspaces, set among fields, pecan groves, and pine stands. In spring we handle denning raccoons and squirrels before litters grow, in summer the calls shift to bats, skunks, and digging animals in the yards, and in fall we seal homes ahead of the winter push. Every Cameron job starts with a full inspection of the roofline, foundation, and crawlspace, and ends with the entries sealed — because in Calhoun County there is always another animal nearby ready to use an open hole.

faqs.q: An opossum keeps getting under my Fort Motte house. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: Opossums den under houses because crawlspaces near Congaree River bluff and floodplain at the county's northern edge are dry, dark, and close to pet food and trash. One opossum is mostly a nuisance; a season of them brings droppings, torn insulation, and fleas. We trap the animal — opossums are handled under depredation rules, since routine relocation is not permitted in South Carolina — then screen vents and repair the crawlspace door so the shelter is gone, not just the tenant.

faqs.q: We have rats in our Fort Motte attic. How is that different from squirrels?
faqs.a: Rats work at night and squirrels work at dawn, which is the first clue. In Fort Motte, roof rats climb from trees, vines, and utility lines around Congaree River bluff and floodplain at the county's northern edge, while Norway rats burrow along foundations and come up through plumbing gaps. We identify the species, trap inside the structure, and seal the entry points at roof and foundation level — poison alone leaves dead rats in walls and does nothing about the openings.

faqs.q: How do you price the work on a Fort Motte home?
faqs.a: Honestly, it depends on what the inspection turns up — and in Fort Motte that is rarely just one hole. Attic contamination, the number of openings to seal in steel, crawlspace repairs, and whether the job needs return visits for trapping all shape the work. We itemize what we find, explain which items stop the problem for good and which are optional, and let you decide with the full list in hand.

Fort Motte.wildlife_intro:
Ask around Fort Motte and the wildlife stories usually trace back to the Congaree River bluff and floodplain at the county's northern edge. Homeowners here phone us first about armadillos in pine-straw beds and lawns, then about opossums in crawlspaces.

Older homes near the town center give way to ranch subdivisions and then to farmhouses on the outskirts, and the wildlife entries change with each ring. Pine straw is the Midlands detail that matters most: copperheads vanish into it, armadillos root through it, and raccoons cross it nightly from creek woods to rooftops.

Before we leave a Fort Motte home, the roofline, foundation line, and any outbuilding we worked on get rechecked opening by opening — that recheck is what keeps one call from becoming three.

faqs.q: How do rats get into Sandy Run homes?
faqs.a: Around Sandy Run, rats follow food and cover: bird feeders, pet food, ivy and brush against the house, and the lines and limbs that reach the roof near I-26 and US 21 corridor farms in the county's northwest. The job is trapping inside, sealing every entry we find, and cutting the routes and food that drew them. We will show you the droppings and rub marks we used to confirm the species, because rat work fails when it is guessed at.

faqs.q: How does bat removal work in Sandy Run?
faqs.a: In Sandy Run, bat work means exclusion only: one-way devices on the main entries, every other opening sealed, and the colony leaves on its own at dusk. South Carolina does not require a permit for bat removal, and we time full exclusions to SCDNR's guidance windows — early spring or August through October — to avoid trapping flightless young during the summer maternity season. Guano cleanup follows once the attic is empty.

faqs.q: What will the crew need to do at my Sandy Run house?
faqs.a: Plan on an inspection first: roofline, attic or crawlspace, and the ground line around the house. From there a Sandy Run job usually combines removing the animal — by one-way eviction or trapping under depredation rules — with sealing, screening, and any cleanup the animal left behind. Jobs near I-26 and US 21 corridor farms in the county's northwest with older construction tend to need more sealing; newer homes often need less. The inspection report is what sets the scope, not a phone guess.
